video_title: Have Billionaires Bought The Midterms? with Issue One's Michael Beckel
gist: Hasan Minhaj and Issue One's Michael Beckel argue campaign finance is legalized corruption: 2026 midterm ads are projected near a record $12B, the top 20 mega donors (led by Andreessen/Horowitz and Musk) have spent $1.2B, and corporate spending has tripled with over half from crypto, online betting, big tech and AI. They detail dark money routing, AIPAC's $100M+ spending, a two-member FEC with no enforcement power, and state-level reforms (Maine, Montana, 25-state amendment calls) Beckel expects to snowball post-Trump.

themes.theme: 2026 midterm money flood: scale and who pays

insights.claim: Political ad spending in the 2026 midterm cycle is projected to hit a record of nearly $12 billion, with at least $1 billion from anonymous donors.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Record ad budgets are a direct revenue tailwind for broadcasters, local TV and digital ad platforms in election years.
insights.quote: political ads are projected to hit a record of nearly $12 billion with at least a billion from anonymous donors

insights.claim: The 2020 and 2024 election cycles each cost about $15 billion, with over $5 billion on each presidential race.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Baseline for sizing election-driven spending cycles.
insights.quote: The 2020 and 2024 election cycles each cost about $15 billion, over 5 billion on each presidential race alone.

insights.claim: The 20 biggest mega donors have put $1.2 billion into 2026 races so far, including about $150 million from Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz and $90 million from Elon Musk.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Venture/tech capital is now among the largest single sources of political money, signaling how much regulatory outcomes are worth to tech.
insights.quote: The 20 biggest mega donors have poured $1.2 billion into races so far.

insights.claim: Direct corporate political spending has more than tripled since the last midterms, with over half coming from crypto, online betting, big tech and AI companies.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Industries with the most regulatory exposure are buying political insurance; expect policy outcomes favorable to crypto, sports betting and AI if this spending works.
insights.quote: direct corporate political spending has more than tripled since the last midterms with over half of spending coming from crypto, online betting, big tech, and AI companies

insights.claim: Elon Musk spent $290 million in 2024 to elect Donald Trump and other Republicans and later claimed that without him Trump would have lost.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Single-donor influence at this scale makes billionaire-politician relationships a material policy and headline risk for their companies.
insights.quote: In 2024, Elon Musk alone spent $290 million to elect Donald Trump and other Republicans.

insights.claim: Secret (dark money) spending in federal elections went from essentially zero before Citizens United to $1.9 billion in the 2024 cycle, up from $1 billion in 2020.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Dark money nearly doubling each cycle means more political spending is untraceable, raising opacity for anyone modeling policy risk.
insights.quote: $1.9 billion. It's billion with a B up from 1 billion in 2020.

insights.claim: Crypto and AI-funded super PACs are spending at least hundreds of millions on politics, dwarfing the sums in the Nixon-era scandals even after inflation adjustment.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: The scale of crypto/AI political spending is unprecedented, implying these sectors view federal policy as existential to valuations.
insights.quote: super PACs now that are funded by AI companies by crypto companies that at a minimum are talking hund00 million in politics

insights.claim: Kamala Harris's 2024 super PAC raised $600 million, of which $300 million came from dark money sources whose funders are unknown.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Both parties depend heavily on opaque money, reducing the odds of quick partisan reform.
insights.quote: raises $600 million. 300 million of it is from dark money that we have no idea who was funding it.

insights.claim: Presidential candidates now raise essentially a billion dollars each across campaigns, allied super PACs and dark money groups, a record that keeps breaking each cycle.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Election spending is structurally growing, not cyclical noise.
insights.quote: raising essentially a billion dollars to run for president between their campaign and their allied super PACs and dark money groups

themes.theme: Industry playbook: crypto, AI and the threat of spending

insights.claim: Citizens United lets industries like crypto and AI tap corporate treasuries for tens or hundreds of millions in ads explicitly supporting or opposing candidates, and they are running that playbook at a new level this cycle.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Corporate treasuries are now a political weapon; regulatory-sensitive sectors can shape who writes their rules.
insights.quote: Now you can tap your corporate treasuries to the tune of tens of millions of dollars, hundreds of millions of dollars and start unleashing ads.

insights.claim: Deep-pocketed players such as AIPAC, AI companies and the crypto industry can contest races almost anywhere, including in states that voted for Trump repeatedly, expanding the competitive map.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Money can manufacture competitiveness, so election outcomes in 'safe' seats become less predictable.
insights.quote: So if you're APAC, if you're the AI companies, if you're the crypto industry, uh when you've got deep pockets, you can take this fight almost anywhere.

insights.claim: The mere threat of a 'tsunami wave' of outside spending makes almost any member of Congress afraid, giving big spenders leverage even without spending.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: The deterrent effect means industry money shapes votes beyond the races it actually funds; watch legislators' positions on crypto/AI rules for this effect.
insights.quote: that threat of being under the tsunami wave of spending also makes almost any member of Congress quiver in their shoes

insights.claim: Outside groups engage in 'battlefield preparation': running ads up to two years early to keep a target's negatives high in seats already known to be competitive, all classified as non-political spending by the IRS.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Political spending is front-loaded and continuous, not just in the final weeks before elections.
insights.quote: Some political operatives call this battlefield preparation.

insights.claim: Dark money flows through three main routes: 501(c)(4)s/501(c)(6)s/LLCs running ads directly, those entities donating to super PACs, and pop-up super PACs formed in the final weeks that don't disclose donors until after election day.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Useful map for tracing who is really funding a political campaign.

insights.claim: Aggressive lawyers advise that 501(c)(4) nonprofits can spend up to 49% of their money on express vote-for/vote-against ads while claiming the other 51% as their primary purpose.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Explains why nonprofit 'social welfare' groups are a major vehicle for anonymous electoral spending.
insights.quote: if you've got a good lawyer, an aggressive lawyer, they might even say you could spend like 49% of your money on ads that say vote for vote against a candidate

insights.claim: Pop-up super PACs that appear in the final couple of weeks before an election need not disclose donors until after election day, because campaign finance laws are antiquated; pending federal legislation would require near-real-time reporting like candidates face.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Late-cycle spending is the least transparent; disclosure reform would close this window.
insights.quote: our campaign finance laws are so antiquated, they're not going to have to disclose their donors until after election day

insights.claim: Super PACs can take any name except a candidate's name, enabling deceptive branding such as Elon Musk's 2024 'RBG PAC', which claimed Ruth Bader Ginsburg would have agreed with Trump on abortion without Musk's name visible to viewers.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Ad messaging is often deliberately misattributed; the true sponsor matters for interpretation.
insights.quote: In uh 2024, Elon Musk funded a group called RBGPAC, which uh was very successful in Pennsylvania.

insights.claim: Candidates coordinate with nominally independent super PACs through 'red boxing', posting the messaging they want emphasized on their websites, which super PAC ads then copy.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: The independence requirement is largely a formality.
insights.quote: this is a technique where candidates feature information on their websites sometimes in a red box like this

themes.theme: Broken referees: Supreme Court and FEC

insights.claim: The FEC is a six-member commission that currently has only two members and needs four votes to investigate or issue rules, leaving it on autopilot as a disclosure-only agency with no enforcement.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Effectively zero federal campaign finance enforcement heading into the midterms, which emboldens aggressive spending tactics.
insights.quote: it's a six-member commission that only has two members on it and it needs four people to agree on anything

insights.claim: The Roberts court has, decision after decision, loosened rules in ways that favor big money, and Beckel agrees that it has effectively legalized corruption by defining it narrowly as quid pro quo.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Judicial relief is unlikely; reform must come through states, ballot measures or constitutional amendment.
insights.quote: The Roberts court has been very okay with the loosening of these rules and decision after decision after decision has made it more favorable for big money

insights.claim: Citizens United's key change was permitting direct corporate independent expenditures, effectively rolling back the 1907 Tillman Act ban on corporate money that followed the Gilded Age.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Today's system resembles the Gilded Age, which historically preceded a major reform wave.
insights.quote: Citizens United made things uniquely bad by allowing direct corporate independent expenditures in politics.

insights.claim: Presidential campaign costs rose from about $114 million in 1976 to $1.4 billion in 2000, driven by soft money, before Citizens United accelerated things further.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Shows the long-run compounding of political spending through every regulatory loophole.
insights.quote: The 1976 presidential election that cost about $114 million. But by 2000, fueled by soft money, that cost had gone up to $1.4 billion.

insights.claim: AIPAC-affiliated groups spent about $46 million on ads in the 2024 cycle, including $14.5 million to defeat Rep. Jamaal Bowman in his primary.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Single-issue groups can decisively swing primaries with concentrated spending.
insights.quote: Apac affiliated groups spent about $46 million in ads, including $14.5 million just to defeat New York Congressman Jamal Bowman

insights.claim: As of early August, AIPAC-affiliated groups had spent over $67 million on 2026 midterm ads, including over $30 million in Michigan to unsuccessfully oppose Abdul El-Sayed, with overall spending above $100 million.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Large spending no longer guarantees wins, indicating diminishing returns as voter sentiment shifts.
insights.quote: including over $30 million in Michigan alone to oppose Abdul Elsay in his primary unsuccessfully

insights.claim: AIPAC spending is becoming a liability in some Democratic primaries: a Gallup poll found Democrats sympathize far more with Palestinians than Israelis, and some candidates now campaign on refusing AIPAC money.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Shifting voter sentiment can turn political money into a negative signal, limiting the power of donors.
insights.quote: A Gallup poll earlier this year found that Democrats now sympathize far more [music] with Palestinians than Israelis.

insights.claim: Voters in some Democratic primaries have rejected candidates despite tens of millions in ad spending, leading Beckel to argue money doesn't decide elections, voters do.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Spending is not perfectly predictive of outcomes, so don't assume the biggest spender wins.
insights.quote: money doesn't decide elections, voters decide elections

insights.claim: A typical House member raises about $3,000 a day for two years, members in the most competitive House races about three times that, and senators in the most competitive races more than $100,000 a day.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Constant donor dependence explains why legislators are receptive to deep-pocketed industries.
insights.quote: your typical member uh of the US House of Representatives is raising about $3,000 a day, okay, for two years.

insights.claim: Members in competitive seats typically spend at least 30 hours a week on fundraising calls from party call centers near Capitol Hill.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Legislators' time is heavily absorbed by donors, reducing bandwidth for policy work.
insights.quote: you're typically talking at least 30 hours a week funding fundraising calls, dialing for dollars

insights.claim: Pennsylvania, Michigan and Ohio are among the most competitive and expensive Senate battlegrounds this cycle, while California's costly media markets make primaries especially expensive.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Ad dollars concentrate in these states' media markets.

themes.theme: Reform pipeline and the post-Trump reset

insights.claim: Issue One predicts a post-Trump wave of campaign finance reform similar to the post-Watergate wave, under its 'Great Reset' campaign.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: A reform cycle could constrain corporate political spending in later years, changing the ROI of industry lobbying.
insights.quote: we think we are probably poised for a a similar slew of reforms that will have to come in this postTrump era

insights.claim: Maine voters passed a ballot measure capping super PAC contributions with 75% support, a direct challenge to the SpeechNow precedent that has inspired federal legislation.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: A likely court test case that could re-open limits on super PAC money.
insights.quote: 75% of Mayers voted for this ballot measure.

insights.claim: A Montana ballot measure this fall would restrict corporate and dark money in elections on the theory that corporations only have powers the state grants them; similar legislation already passed in Hawaii with near-unanimous bipartisan support.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: State corporate-charter law is an emerging route to curbing corporate election spending without overturning Citizens United.
insights.quote: companies only have the powers that are granted to them by the state

insights.claim: 25 states, most recently Oklahoma, Idaho and Utah, have called on Congress to pass a constitutional amendment allowing regulation of money in politics, and Republican Rep. Tom Barrett introduced the first Republican-led campaign finance amendment.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Bipartisan support for a constitutional fix is building, though passage remains a long shot.
insights.quote: there are now 25 states. That's half of the entire country

insights.claim: Obama in 2008 became the first major-party nominee to reject general-election public financing (capped near $84 million), outspent McCain, and no major nominee has used the system since.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Public financing at the federal level is effectively dead without modernization, so private money dominates.
insights.quote: no major party nominee since then has participated in this system

insights.claim: Seattle's 'democracy dollars' program mails residents four $25 vouchers to give to city council candidates, an experiment in alternatives to big-donor funding.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckel (Issue One)
insights.so_what: Local public-financing experiments are the testbed for future national reforms.
insights.quote: They call them democracy dollars in Seattle

insights.claim: Congressional stock trading remains legal despite broad public opposition, and Hasan claims Trump made more stock trades in his first year back than all members of Congress combined.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: A stock-trading ban remains a live reform with bipartisan public support that could change insider-trading-style signals from political trades.
insights.quote: made more stock trades than all members of Congress combined
